hints: Notice the jet has cross-sectional area $A$ and speed $v$, so in time $t$ a cylinder of length $vt$ and volume $Avt$ reaches the wall.
Connect mass to that volume using density $\rho$, so the mass arriving per second is $\rho A v$.
Use force as rate of change of horizontal momentum, where each mass loses all its horizontal velocity $v$ because it does not rebound.
walkthrough: Volume hitting the wall in time $t$ is the cylinder swept out by the jet: $V = A \times vt = Avt$.
Mass of this water is $m = \rho V = \rho Avt$, so mass per unit time is $m/t = \rho A v$ with unit $\text{kg s}^{-1}$.
Each kilogram arrives with horizontal momentum $v$ and leaves with zero horizontal momentum because the water does not rebound and spreads sideways.
By Newton's second law, force on water equals rate of loss of momentum: $F = (m/t) \times (v - 0) = (\rho A v) \times v$.
Hence $F = \rho A v^2$, and by Newton's third law this is also the force on the wall. This is option D.

options.A: Dividing by $A$ is wrong dimensionally and ignores that larger area means more mass hitting per second.
options.B: Dividing by $A$ is incorrect; mass per second increases with $A$, so force must increase with $A$.
options.C: This is the rate of mass hitting the wall, but force needs mass rate multiplied by velocity change $v$.
options.D: Mass per second $\rho A v$ multiplied by velocity lost $v$ gives force $\rho A v^2$.
